http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09212v1.title: On the Limits of Execution Traces for Repairing Assertion Failures in LLM-Generated Code
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09212v1.abstract: Iterative repair returns a failed program's error to a large language model (LLM) and asks it to fix it. After iterative repair, the remaining failures are mostly assertion failures: with four Qwen2.5 models, they make up 79% of residual failures on BigCodeBench, all on HumanEval and 93% on LiveCodeBench. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08666v1.title: Pdb or Not to Be: Comparing Debugging Interfaces With Pass$_{X}$@$k$
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08666v1.abstract: Interactive debuggers are indispensable to human software development, yet coding agents overwhelmingly rely on edit-execute-observe loops, using common bash tools, test scripts, and print statements to debug via repeated shell commands. Stepping through a debugger provides live access to runtime state, which may enable different problem-solving capabilities. However, prior work typically introduces the debugger as an additional tool or through a new subagent, making its individual contribution difficult to isolate from the associated scaffold changes. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09177v1.title: Analyzing Code Provenance in LLMs for Programming Education
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09177v1.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) play an increasing role in programming education, challenging traditional assessment methods as they can generate fully functional code instantly. This disrupts the reliability of student submissions as indicators of learning and effort. To address this issue, code provenance is essential for tracing the origins of code and distinguishing student-authored, AI-generated, and externally sourced components. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08811v1.abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) are one of the key components of current agentic systems. LRMs augment their output with an explicit chain-of-thought reasoning stage, introducing a new attack surface for thought injection, in which untrusted text resembling the model's own deliberation is fed back to the model. We present a two-part study of this attack, performed against the prevailing large, production class open-weight models (e.g., GLM-5.3, MiniMax-M2.5, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next). http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08947v1.abstract: Translating parallel scientific codes between HPC programming frameworks is a critical but labor-intensive task. Existing LLM-based approaches rely on fixed sequential pipelines with undifferentiated repair strategies and correctness criteria that do not match scientific computing practice. We present an agent-skill framework that separates translation, compilation diagnosis, and execution validation into three autonomous agents coordinated by a verdict-driven orchestrator, routing each failure to a targeted repair skill rather than retrying blindly. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09113v1.abstract: LLM agents can exceed their authorization boundaries while pursuing user goals without an adversary. We formalize this phenomenon as authorization drift across data, tool, scope, and time, and introduce the Authorization Drift Benchmark (ADB): 648 samples across seven domains, each pairing a sufficient compliant path with an attractive unauthorized shortcut. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08905v1.abstract: As language agents tackle increasingly complex tasks, they increasingly rely on multiple agents to coordinate specialized work, requiring decisions not only about what each subagent should do but also which tools and workspace resources it should access. Existing agent systems provide mechanisms for controlling tools and execution environments, but do not directly specify the resources required by each delegated subtask. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09802v1.abstract: LLM-based coding agents such as Claude Code are guided by repository instruction files (also called context files or agent configuration files) like AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md, which are read in every agent session. As any documentation artifact, these files can fall behind the code and become stale (e.g., a test folder moves, but the file still points to the old one). In technical debt terms, such a stale instruction is documentation debt, and its interest is the cost it adds to every later agent session. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08644v1.title: Decision Context: Persistent Behavioral Learning for AI Agents
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08644v1.abstract: LLM agents do not learn from corrections across sessions. A user fixes the same mistake at the start of every conversation. Existing agent memory systems primarily handle facts, such as preferences, entities, and conversational history, rather than procedural knowledge. We present Forge Decision Context (forge_dc), a system that captures behavioral signals from human corrections and self-assessed tool-call failures, compiles them into imperative RULE directives, and injects them at the decision points where they apply. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09825v1.title: BitDecoding-FP4: Native FP4 KV Cache Decoding via Algorithm-System Co-Design
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09825v1.abstract: The key-value (KV) cache dominates memory capacity and bandwidth in long-context LLM serving. While 4-bit microscaling formats (NVFP4, MXFP4) shrink the cache and run attention on FP4 Tensor Cores, a fundamental gap remains between algorithmic quantization and system-aware acceleration: existing FP4 KV systems use vanilla quantization that causes severe accuracy drops, whereas accuracy-oriented 4-bit algorithms rely on vector codebooks whose lookup overhead degrades decoding throughput. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09791v1.abstract: Competitive programming problems pose distinctive challenges for Large Language Models, as they demand not only proficient code generation but also advanced algorithmic reasoning. This study presents a Retrieval-Augmented Generation approach specifically designed to enhance the capacity of Large Language Models to address such problems. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09291v1.title: AutoRefine: Auto-Calibrating Code Judges from Workflow Outcomes
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09291v1.abstract: LLM judges increasingly serve as quality gates for code changes that have no test oracle, but a judge prompt must be calibrated for its task and recalibrated as the system it judges evolves, while hand labels for the calibration are resource intensive and go stale. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09382v1.abstract: Weight-Space Programming (WSP) enables reasoning agents to directly inspect and modify neural network parameters, offering an alternative to gradient-based model adaptation. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08647v1.title: IWIBench: Evaluating Gradient-Free Model Driven Intra-weight Injection
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08647v1.abstract: Intra-weight injection lets one model change another model's behaviour by editing its weights directly, without gradients. Despite growing interest in these approaches, there has been no systematic way to evaluate how well models perform them. We introduce IWIBench, which measures a large editor model's ability to modify the weights of a smaller target model (typically Gemma 3 4B IT) to achieve one of ten classical text-editing objectives while preserving its other capabilities. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08768v1.title: Conflux: Preventing Privilege Escalation with Principal Contexts and System-Level Evaluation
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08768v1.abstract: LLM agents combine information from multiple principals while acting externally. Model-level defences remain probabilistic, so enforcement must sit outside model judgement. We present Conflux, a principal-context defence. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.10469v1.abstract: Local AI promises capable personal assistants that run on users' own devices, keeping data and computation under their control. Open-weight models that fit on local devices can now handle practical tasks such as coding. Yet current inference engines fall short. Popular engines such as vLLM and SGLang target datacenter GPUs with dedicated host memory, while local engines underuse the memory hierarchy of unified-memory devices. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.12835v1.abstract: As large language models become more capable agents, they can exhibit deceptive behaviors, cheating human for higher rewards while appearing helpful. We attribute this failure to evaluation-side partial observability, where models are evaluated mainly from final outcome, without checking the faithfulness of underlying reasoning, tool use, and environmental effects. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11560v1.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents acting across web applications and online services often need multi-turn corrections to align their work with users' underspecified goals and preferences. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.10542v1.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly improve themselves through self-evolution, distilling execution experience into persistent, reusable skills. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11929v1.title: Can LLM Agents Organize Their Own Memory?
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11929v1.abstract: In most LLM agents, weights are fixed after deployment, so new information must be retained in external memory. Existing approaches often rely on predefined records and fixed organizational rules, which cannot readily accommodate evolving tasks and interactions. This raises the question: can LLM agents organize their own memory using ordinary documents? We introduce self-organized memory (SoMem), a framework that stores memory in linked documents. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.10240v1.abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents accumulate sessions of up to millions of tokens, far more key-value (KV) cache than one GPU holds, so serving systems keep a small budget of tokens and evict the rest. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11581v1.title: Same Error, Different Recovery: How Delivery Changes LLM Agent Behavior
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11581v1.abstract: A tool-using language model must decide whether to retry a failed call, correct it, or stop and tell the user. The error text alone may not be enough: the same feedback can lead to different actions depending on where it appears in the conversation. We isolate this delivery problem by varying placement, guidance, retained history and turn structure. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.10404v1.abstract: Frontier agentic LLMs are trained on verifiable rewards in reinforcement learning (RL) environments built from real software repositories. A passing test suite is treated as the reward for solving the task. We show that, on hard problems, frontier models often satisfy these rewards by obtaining the answer instead of deriving it, known as reward hacking. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11330v1.title: When Credit Turns Against Tools: Transition-Aware Credit Assignment in Agentic Reinforcement Learning
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11330v1.abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards trains language models through multi-turn tool interactions, yet their reasoning performance and tool-calling ability can decline during training. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.12122v1.abstract: AI agent harnesses play the critical role of providing LLMs with an interface to a computing environment. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.10884v1.abstract: Much of the automation handed to language-model agents is procedural: each step needs little intelligence, but a long unattended run must follow a skill or SOP stated once at the start. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11266v1.abstract: As enterprises delegate consequential work to multi-agent LLM systems, benign-looking requests can escalate into unsafe actions as they propagate across sessions through poisoned shared state, long-context documents, and trusted peer messages: no single message is malicious, yet the assembled tool action is. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11861v1.title: Scaling Adaptive Prompt Injection Attacks with Agent Swarms
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11861v1.abstract: Prompt injections have emerged as one of the top security risks faced by AI agents today. Early work in prompt injection attacks looked at simple tool-call agents and static attack payloads, and were saturated since mid-2025. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14320v1.abstract: External memory enables LLM agents to improve from experience by distilling trajectories of past tasks into concise lessons for new tasks. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13144v1.abstract: Effective teaching requires reasoning about the learner as well as the task, a capacity that Theory of Mind describes as inferring another agent's latent state from its behavior. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13509v1.abstract: Small language models (SLMs) running on mobile devices can keep user data private and work without connectivity. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13412v1.title: Bursts That Outlast Themselves: Persistent Degradation in Prefix-Cached Agent Serving

http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14356v1.title: EngineAgent: Agentizing On-Device LLM Inference Engines with Inference Stack Hierarchy Awareness and Hardware Abilities

http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13541v1.abstract: Data-science and ML-engineering agents are evaluated on benchmarks such as MLE-bench, ALE-Bench, SWE-fficiency and AlgoTune, whose tasks yield a quantity (a Kaggle metric, contest score or speedup).
